units: the price of a handmade piece of furniture comes from several sources
the raw material bought from the supplier counts towards it
the joiner's tools wear down and have to be replaced
the solid wood bench used for shaping decays with use
the craftsman's skill is acquired through long practice
the beginner copies that skill imperfectly
the customer's wait matches a stretch with no money coming in
no single one of these sources justifies the sum asked
text: Walk into a joiner's workshop and ask where the price of a finished cabinet actually comes from. Several answers hold true at the same time. There is the timber, chosen, seasoned and paid for at the supplier's door. There are the planes and the clamps, which lose their edge and must be bought again. There is the bench itself, a heavy slab of wood that wears away quietly under years of shaping. There is the hand of the craftsman, slow to acquire, and the hand of the beginner still copying it badly. And there is the waiting the customer agrees to, a stretch of weeks in which no money comes in. Not one of these on its own explains the figure on the label. The buyer who calls it steep is looking at a smooth polished board; the maker sees behind it the whole run of costs that brought it there.

units: the head of the team kept a record of operations
the foundations progressed at the planned rate in the first week
a steel delivery arrived incomplete the following week
the load calculation had to be redone beam by beam
the supplier blamed a break in supply
an engineer suggested replacing the section with an equivalent one held in stock
the substitution was approved on condition that the slab be strengthened
the rate of output fell before it settled
the extra cost showed up on the final invoice
text: The foreman in charge of the site kept a logbook, and every operation went into it in the order it happened. Through the first week the foundations rose at exactly the rate planned. The week after, a steel delivery turned up short. The load calculation had to be worked through again, beam by beam, before anything else could be poured. The supplier put the blame on a break in supply. At the technical meeting an engineer suggested swapping the missing section for an equivalent one already held in the yard, and the substitution went through on one condition: the slab was to be strengthened. Once work resumed, output dropped a notch, hung there a while and then settled. The logbook holds the record of all of it, and the final invoice told the same story in the shape of an extra cost.

units: a written estimate must be asked for before a repair is started
an agreement made only in speech protects neither side
the document must set out the work, the materials and the time announced
the sum paid in advance ties the customer to the trader
the trader may not keep that advance if the job has not begun
proofs of payment form the basis of a claim
any change decided while the work runs must be notified in writing
the final bill must be compared point by point with the accepted estimate
text: Ask for a written estimate before any substantial piece of repair work begins. A promise made only in conversation protects neither of the two sides once a dispute starts. The document should set out the work to be carried out, the materials involved and the time the trader has announced. Look closely at the deposit clause: money handed over in advance binds the customer to the trader, though the trader may not keep it if the job has never begun. Keep every proof of payment you are given, since a claim will rest on those and on nothing else. If anything changes while the work is under way, put the change in writing and have it acknowledged. Then compare the closing bill with the estimate you accepted, point by point. A gap nobody can account for is fair ground to refuse to pay.

units: a storage building has been running slowly since it lost its main client
orders have fallen sharply
part of the workforce has moved onto reduced hours
seasonal recruitment has been halted
nearby haulage firms fear knock-on effects
sharing the building between several shippers is under consideration
converting the floor space calls for automated sorting equipment
the local authority would pay for half of that equipment
a first occupier is said to have signed a promise of lease
text: A storage building on the industrial estate has been running well below capacity since it lost its main client. Those in charge describe a steep fall in orders that has left the loading bays bare and the forklifts standing idle. Some of the workforce has moved onto reduced hours, and the seasonal recruitment planned for the coming months has been halted. Haulage firms nearby fear the effect will travel down the line to them as well. One idea is currently under study: share the building between several medium-sized shippers instead of depending on a single customer. Converting the floor space would call for automated sorting equipment, half of it paid for by the local authority. A first occupier is said to have signed a promise of lease, which would reopen hiring by the busy season.

units: the two aisles of the covered market do not run at the same rhythm
the fruit seller calls out to passers-by and announces his prices aloud
he drops a price as soon as goods risk spoiling
the cheese shop ages its products in a cellar
its displayed prices rarely change
perishable goods force selling in a hurry
a product that improves with age allows waiting
the first business takes on seasonal hands during the glut
the second keeps the same employee all year
text: Have a look at the two aisles of the covered market: they do not run at the same speed at all. Down the first one the fruit seller shouts at whoever walks past, calls his prices out over the crates and drops one the moment a tray looks like turning. Down the second the cheese shop keeps its stock ageing in a cellar, writes small quiet labels and hardly ever moves a price. The one of them sells freshness, so he lives in a hurry; the other sells patience, so he can afford to wait for his buyer. You will notice too that the first takes on extra hands when the harvest floods in, while the second keeps the same assistant all year round. Two shops standing side by side, two opposite ways of making a living. The goods set the rhythm, and the rhythm decides what ends up in the till.

units: the argument about funding social protection overlooks three aspects
the deduction from wages is felt as a tax imposed from above
that deduction in fact pays for shared cover
the uneven earnings of the self-employed make any fixed scale unfair
the protection of the self-employed remains incomplete
some employers escape the deductions by using short contracts
farming work out to others adds to that avoidance
the writer holds that the question is one of fairness and not of bookkeeping
text: Three things go missing from the whole argument about how social protection is paid for, and they are rarely named together. The first of them is the deduction taken from wages. It feels like a tax imposed from above, when what it actually buys is cover shared among everyone. The second is the standing of the self-employed: earnings that swing from month to month make any fixed scale unfair, and their protection is still full of holes. The third, and the quietest, is the employers who slip out of paying by stacking up short contracts and farming the work out to others. Each of these turns on fairness rather than on bookkeeping. Those calling for lighter charges skirt the first; those defending the present arrangement skirt the third. Name the three pieces first, and then decide.

units: the oldest hand in the bindery joined it very young as a beginner
she was put first on cleaning and then on folding the sections
the mixing of the glues was handed to her next
she spent long seasons at the same finishing bench
she bought the customer list when the house nearly disappeared
that purchase was paid for out of her savings and two loans
she trained about a dozen young people
several of her pupils now run shops of their own
she passed the business to her last pupil, asking him not to sell cheap
text: The oldest hand in the bindery came to the place very young, as a beginner, back when leather was still sewn by hand from one end to the other. She was given the sweeping first, then the folding of the sections, and later the mixing of the glues. She stood at the same finishing bench for season after season, long enough for the top of it to hold the marks of her tools. When the house nearly went under, she bought the customer list herself, with her savings and two small loans. After that she trained a good dozen young people, several of whom now run shops of their own. Too tired at last for the press, she handed the business to her final pupil, asking one thing of him only: never sell the work cheap. She still comes in to sit by the window, and puts a word on a loose stitch.

units: the equipment recently fitted to the assembly line draws a divided opinion
tightening is driven electronically and its accuracy is not disputed
that accuracy removes the rework tied to tightening by hand
the machine now sets the pace for the operator
a badly seated part locks the station and blocks the stations before it
the shop has gained steadiness and lost flexibility
upkeep calls for electronic skills the team does not have
every breakdown means waiting for someone from outside
the share of faulty parts has dropped sharply
text: Opinion on the equipment recently fitted to the assembly line is a divided one, and reasonably so. Tightening is driven electronically now and its accuracy is beyond any argument; the rework that came with tightening by hand has simply gone away. What comes along with it is a pace set by the machine rather than by the operator. Since the cycle no longer pauses on its own, one badly seated part locks the station, and the stoppage travels back to every station before it. The shop as a whole has bought steadiness at the price of give. Upkeep has changed as well: it asks for electronic skills the team does not have, so every breakdown means waiting for someone from outside. The balance still tips the right way, because the share of faulty parts coming off the line has dropped sharply.

units: the writer ordered a kitchen and signed a detailed estimate
a deposit was paid when the order was placed
no indication of delivery has been given since
three dates in turn were announced and then missed
the writer's last message went unanswered
the writer has to rent a furnished flat, which raises his costs
he asks either for a written commitment to a firm date with compensation
or else for the deposit to be returned in full within a fortnight
he says the file will go to a consumer body if no agreement is reached
text: I am writing to you once again about the kitchen I ordered from your shop at the start of the season. I signed a detailed estimate at the time and paid the deposit you asked for, and since then not one word has reached me about delivery. Your staff have named three dates in turn, every one of which has passed, and my last message went unanswered. Because of all this I am having to rent a furnished flat, and the cost of that grows with every week that passes. Let me put a reasonable way out of this to you. Either you commit in writing to a firm fitting date, with a reduction covering what the delay has cost me, or you return the deposit in full within a fortnight. Failing an agreement between us, the file goes to the consumer body that is already handling my case. Yours faithfully.

units: the choice between an employee and a self-employed contractor comes up often in small firms
the contractor's invoice takes the place of the wage and the employer's contributions
the contractor looks cheaper in the short term
the contractor bills for each job separately
the employee takes on unplanned tasks at no extra charge
the training the employee receives then benefits the firm that paid for it
an exclusive and lasting arrangement with a contractor risks reclassification
the advice is to keep contracting for one-off and specialised needs
the advice is to hire for the core activity
text: Is it better to take someone on as staff or to bring in a self-employed contractor? Small firms keep asking the question, and the answer turns on what you set side by side. On immediate cost the contractor looks cheaper, since an invoice takes the place of a wage and of the employer's contributions. Over time the gap narrows: the contractor bills for each job, while the employee picks up whatever comes up unplanned at no extra charge. And loyalty? That leans clearly towards hiring, because the training paid for by the firm stays inside the firm. Legal risk runs the other way, though: an exclusive, long-running arrangement with a contractor can be reclassified. So which? Keep contracting for one-off, specialised needs, and hire for the work that sits at the heart of the business.
